clue.text: Band tour on back of success on-line?

indicators.note: the back of a word is the letter it finishes on, so one letter comes out of it and no more

parts.note: the last letter of success, standing at the back of the word
a tour is a trip
e- is the prefix for anything done online, as in email and e-commerce

explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' looks like the musicians whose tour this is, and means a coloured strip. The e- prefix for online is worth banking — setters use it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: A stripe is a band of colour running across something, so the two words name the same marking — one on a flag, the other on cloth.

clue.text: Break crockery up

indicators.note: a down entry read upward runs from its final square to its first, so the letters arrive in the opposite order

parts.note: crockery is pots, and a down clue reads them from the bottom up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' is doing noun duty — a break in play — while the surface has you smashing plates. A down entry has no backwards, which is why the clue says up.
explanation.definitionFit: A break in a journey and a stop are the same pause, so the noun senses match exactly; nothing here is telling you to halt.

clue.text: Those stopping football and cricket desist

parts.note: the man who stops a football match is the ref
what stops a cricket match is rain

explanation.walkthrough: One phrase, 'those stopping', serves two utterly different stoppers — a man in black and the weather — and the answer they build is a third kind of stopping.
explanation.definitionFit: To refrain from something is to hold back from doing it, which is what desist means: both are verbs for stopping yourself.

clue.text: Maybe Labour overturned Liberal legislation's divisive feature

parts.note: Labour is one party among several, and 'maybe' is what sends you up to the general word

indicators.note: what has been tipped end over end sits the other way up, so these letters are read from the far end back

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for Liberal
legislation is the law, and it follows the L before the pair are turned

explanation.walkthrough: The Westminster surface is a decoy — nothing political is overturned here, and the second half of the answer is a builder's word, not a parliament's.
explanation.definitionFit: A party wall is the single wall two adjoining houses share, so it is the structure that divides one home from the next.

clue.text: Propose splitting amount that's coughed up

indicators.note: to split a thing is to open it and get between its halves, so the other word lands in the middle rather than alongside

parts.note: an amount of money is a sum
to put a motion to a meeting is to propose it

explanation.walkthrough: A committee-room surface, where proposals and amounts belong, hides a word from the sickbed; nothing sounds like an instruction until 'splitting' turns literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sputum is the medical name for matter brought up from the lungs by coughing, so the phrase describes it exactly.

clue.text: Advice from below about where to fix rope

indicators.note: in a down clue, from below means the word is read upwards from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: a tip is a piece of advice
on means about, concerning, as in a talk on birds

explanation.surface: A climber shouts advice up from beneath about where to anchor the rope.
explanation.walkthrough: TIP read 'from below' becomes PIT, and ON is 'about' in the sense of concerning.
explanation.definitionFit: A piton is a metal spike that climbers hammer into rock to secure a rope.

clue.text: Stretched nurses down for shifts this evening

indicators.note: to nurse someone is to hold them in your care, so the outer word closes round what it is looking after

parts.note: a stretched rope is tight
anyone down for shifts is on — the crossword's ON for working or on duty

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here is medical: 'nurses' means holding rather than caring, and ON for working is a piece of shorthand worth banking early.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonight is the night of the day you are standing in, which is what this evening means — the same stretch of hours under two names.

clue.text: Chief planner furious about M1, forbidding bridges

indicators.note: words written about a subject run all the way round it, so this one opens and closes over what follows

parts.note: furious is mad, and it opens after its MA

indicators.note: a bridge spans what lies beneath it, so the word doing the bridging takes the other one inside

parts.note: a forbidding look is a stern one
the motorway's 1 is the Roman numeral I, so M1 is written MI

explanation.walkthrough: A road scheme with a bridge over the motorway is a complete decoy, and reading the 1 as a Roman numeral is the step that unlocks it.
explanation.definitionFit: The mastermind of an operation is the one who plans it while everyone else follows, so 'chief planner' is that job in plain words.

clue.text: Drone maybe brought into harbour after power failure

parts.note: might is power, as in might is right

indicators.note: whatever is brought into a place ends up inside it, so the short word is carried into the middle of the long one

parts.note: a harbour is a haven, and it opens after HAVE
a drone is one kind of bee, which is what 'maybe' signals

explanation.walkthrough: 'Power failure' reads as one phrase and is really two jobs: the first word is wordplay, the second the definition. Spotting that seam is the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A might-have-been is someone whose promise never came to anything, which is the sharper sense of failure — a person, not an event.

clue.text: Sheep anti/pro low cloud

parts.note: of the pros and cons, con is the anti side
to be pro something is to be for it
cloud down at ground level is mist

explanation.walkthrough: The slash makes 'anti/pro' look like one hesitation rather than two words pulling opposite ways, and each of them is a separate piece of the build.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone called a sheep follows the flock without thinking, which is exactly what a conformist does — the metaphor, not the animal.

clue.text: Backing lost for nosy US agency

indicators.note: what is lost has gone missing from the word, so the letter named never reaches the answer

parts.note: nosy means of the nose — nasal — and without that L the agency is left
the backing is the last letter, and here that letter is L

explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing lost' reads as a sponsor pulling out of a deal, and is an instruction to drop a final letter — the only operation in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: NASA is the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the American government body that runs spaceflight, known everywhere by its initials.

clue.text: Gay in Ghent so upset there are no bars

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of these words fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A gay man in Ghent is upset that the town has no bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' suggests pubs in the surface, but here it means prohibitions; the twelve letters of 'Gay in Ghent so' are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said when anything is permitted, with no restrictions, which is what having no bars means.

clue.text: Shapelessness misrepresented by outlines

indicators.note: misrepresented means presented wrongly, so the letters of the two words are set out in a different order

explanation.surface: Something formless has been badly drawn by its outlines.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of 'by outlines' rearranged give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Nebulosity is cloudiness or vagueness, a lack of clear form, so it is a kind of shapelessness.

clue.text: Protruding part goddess squeezes back in

indicators.note: squeezes means the goddess's name holds the reversed letters tightly inside it

parts.note: Hera was the queen of the Greek gods

indicators.note: back means the little word in is read backwards

explanation.surface: A goddess squeezes a sticking-out bit back in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in' reads as one phrase, pushing something back, but 'back' reverses IN to NI, which Hera squeezes between HER and A.
explanation.definitionFit: A hernia is a bulge where an organ pushes through the wall of the cavity holding it, so it protrudes.

clue.text: Explosive combat involved great sacrifice

parts.note: HE is the standard abbreviation for high explosive

indicators.note: involved in the sense of twisted or convoluted, so the letters of combat are tangled into a new order

explanation.surface: An explosive battle has cost many lives, a great sacrifice in war.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Explosive' looks like an adjective for the combat but gives HE; 'involved' then rearranges COMBAT into CATOMB.
explanation.definitionFit: A hecatomb was originally an ancient Greek offering of a hundred oxen, and now means any large-scale slaughter.

clue.text: Fake tea the French turn brown

parts.note: char is the old British slang for a cup of tea
'the' in French is la
to tan is to turn brown in the sun

explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' for LA or LE is a workhorse of British cryptics. 'Turn brown' is a verb where the surface offers it as a description of the tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A charlatan is someone passing as an expert they are not, so 'Fake' names the person rather than a forged object.

clue.text: Five plus Burgess, say, turned communist once

indicators.note: a thing turned has been spun end for end, so the assembled letters are read from the far end back

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
plus in the sense of and also
Guy Burgess was the Cambridge spy, and 'say' warns that the first name is only one example of the surname

explanation.walkthrough: Burgess is a decoy and a gift at once: the spy is real, and all the clue wants from him is a first name that doubles as a word for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Yugoslavia was a communist federation that broke up in the 1990s, so its people were citizens of a communist state that no longer exists.

clue.text: Fuel supply cook uncapped successfully

indicators.note: uncapped means with the cap, the top letter in a down clue, removed

parts.note: to boil is to cook
well means successfully, as in 'it went well'

explanation.surface: A cook takes the lid off and things go well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncapped' takes the first letter off BOIL, leaving OIL; in a down clue the first letter is the cap.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil well extracts petroleum, so it is a source supplying fuel.

clue.text: Somewhat peculiar man in expensive clothes

indicators.note: somewhat means only part of what follows, and the part meant is an unbroken run of letters inside it

parts.note: the run begins inside peculiAR and finishes on the I of in

explanation.walkthrough: Three ordinary words hide a designer label across their joins, and 'Somewhat' is the only hint that nothing needs rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Armani is the Italian fashion house whose suits cost a fortune, so the label's name stands in for the garments themselves.

clue.text: Building work that near bores old PM

indicators.note: to bore is to drive a hole right into something, so whatever bores ends up inside it

parts.note: Theresa May was prime minister until 2019
not that big and not so big say the same thing
nr is the map-maker's short form of near

explanation.walkthrough: 'That' as SO is the piece to spot: the smallest word in the clue, doing the most work, hidden in plain grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: Masonry is what a mason produces — stone or brick laid into walls — so 'building work' names the trade by its finished product.

clue.text: Walter fixes shoes for Spooner's runs

indicators.note: Spooner's version means the starting sounds of the two words are swapped, after the Rev Spooner

parts.note: Wally is a familiar form of the name Walter, said 'wolly' in British speech
a cobbler cobbles, that is mends, shoes

explanation.surface: A cobbler called Walter mends footwear.
explanation.walkthrough: Wally cobbles, with the opening sounds swapped, becomes the answer. Spoonerisms, named after the Rev William Spooner, swap the initial sounds of two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The collywobbles is an informal word for an upset stomach or nervous queasiness, which can mean the runs.

clue.text: OK without sealing airlock regularly

indicators.note: to seal a container is to close it round its contents, so the outer letters shut over what sits between them

parts.note: w/o is the everyday written shorthand for without

indicators.note: taken at regular intervals means every second letter rather than all of them

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of aIrLoCk

explanation.walkthrough: The airlock and the seal belong to one picture, which is what makes them so hard to read as instructions instead of scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilco is radio shorthand for 'will comply', the operator's way of saying OK — message received and it will be done.

clue.text: Somebody catching cold at any time

indicators.note: to catch a thing is to close your hand round it, so the letter is held inside rather than added at the end

parts.note: somebody, an unnamed person, is one
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as marked on a tap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Catching cold' is a single idea on the surface and two instructions underneath, which is why nothing in the sentence sounds mechanical.
explanation.definitionFit: In 'if once you doubt them', once means ever — at any time at all; that conditional sense is older than the counting one.

clue.text: Tool store

definitions.meaning: the rasp in the toolbox, for smoothing metal
papers put away where they can be found again

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions and no joinery at all: the shortest clue in the puzzle, and the seam between its halves is the only thing to find.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the metal rasp that smooths a surface; the other is papers kept in order, the drawer and the act of putting them there.

clue.text: US cop that is blocking tunnel at ground

indicators.note: something blocking a passage sits inside it, so these letters go within the others
ground as in crushed or milled, so the letters of tunnel at are broken up and remixed

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A police officer stands at ground level where something is obstructing a tunnel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' turns TUNNEL AT into LUTENANT, and 'blocking' puts IE inside it after the L. In American police forces a lieutenant is a rank above sergeant.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieutenant is a rank of police officer in US departments, above sergeant and below captain.

clue.text: Cry quietly having dispatched one large lemon?

parts.note: a cry is a yell

indicators.note: to dispatch a thing is to send it away for good, so the letter named leaves the assembly

parts.note: speaking low is speaking quietly
large is L on a clothing label, and one of the two Ls is sent away

explanation.walkthrough: Run the two pieces together and there are three Ls in a row; the clue sends one of them away, which is all 'one large' is there for.
explanation.definitionFit: Lemon names the colour by the fruit that owns it, and the question mark admits the fruit is only one example of the shade.

clue.text: Stimulating stuff from lead characters in naughty novel, I'm told

indicators.note: I'm told means as heard, so the letters are said aloud

parts.words: lead characters in naughty novel, I'm
parts.note: the lead characters of naughty and novel are two Ns, said as 'ens', followed by I'm

explanation.surface: Someone has heard that a racy novel is a real stimulant.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of naughty and novel are N and N, said 'ens'; add I'm and say it aloud. 'lead characters' looks like the novel's heroes, but these are letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An enzyme is a protein catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions in the body, so it stimulates them.
